title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
hook: the fierce god's gentlest names: Shankara and Shambhu, the ones who make things well

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened the Shiva Sahasranama, the hymn of Shiva's names, and met Sthanu, the steady post. What other name did you hear someone you love go by? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

What do you call someone who frightens people and is still the one they run to? Shiva sits in cremation grounds, smeared with ash, a snake around his neck. Yesterday the list of his names gave us Bhima, the fearsome one. And yet, painted on bus windshields and sung at temple doors, the names you'll hear are soft ones. Shambho. Shankara. Two names from the same hymn, and they don't sound frightening at all. Today's selection from the Shiva Sahasranama is the gentle side of a fierce god.
screen: `FEARSOME, AND STILL RUN TO.` → `SHAMBHO. SHANKARA.` → `THE GENTLE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Start with Shankara. Tradition explains the name as the one who makes well-being: sham is ease, welfare, peace, and kara is the one who makes it. Shambhu sits right beside it, explained as the one from whom well-being comes. Say them slowly and they almost sound like comfort. The same names turn up in a Vedic hymn to Rudra, the Shri Rudram, still chanted in temples. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, and to his arrows. It doesn't pretend he's harmless. But deep into the hymn, it turns, and bows to him as Shambhu, as Shankara, and as Shiva, the auspicious one, and then as the one more auspicious still. That's where the words namah shivaya are heard, bowing to Shiva, inside a hymn that began by facing his anger. So when the sahasranama gives a devotee Bhima and Shankara in the same breath, it isn't confused. It's keeping the old pattern: the fierce one and the kind one are the same one. Some of us know this from our own lives. The aunt with the sharp tongue who drove across town when you were sick. The coach who scared you and then believed in you. A name like Shankara doesn't erase the fierceness. It says what the fierceness is for. In the stories, Shiva's terrible side burns away what harms, and what's left is well-being. A devotee who says Shankara is naming the end of that story, not just the middle.
screen: `SHANKARA: THE MAKER OF WELL-BEING.` · `SHAMBHU: WELL-BEING COMES FROM HIM.` · `THE RUDRAM: FROM ANGER TO SHIVA.` · `FIERCE AND KIND, THE SAME ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask your sharp edge what it guards. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one fierce thing in yourself: a quick temper, a stubborn streak, a no you say fast. Don't sand it down. Ask it, quietly: what are you protecting? Wait. An answer may come as a person, a value, a tender place. On each out-breath, let the edge stay, and let it turn toward what it guards. If you pray, you can say Shankara or Shambho as you breathe out. If not, just let the breath carry the question. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's names from it: Shankara, the one who makes well-being, and Shambhu, from whom well-being comes. Fierce and kind, the same one.

Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Today, think of one fierce person in your life, and name, just to yourself, what their fierceness has protected. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Devotees greet Shiva with names like Shambho and Shankara in songs, chants and everyday speech, and the Shri Rudram, with its line namah shivaya, is chanted in Shiva temples, especially during abhisheka, the bathing of the linga.

notes: Selection two of seven. Glosses: Shankara 'the one who makes well-being' (sham + kara) and Shambhu 'the one from whom well-being comes', presented as 'usually explained'. These follow standard lexicons (Monier-Williams). Confirm both are in the Mahabharata list and the glosses.

Shri Rudram: opening bows to Rudra's anger and arrows ('namaste rudra manyava ...'); the eighth section bows to Shambhu, Shankara, Shiva and 'shivatara' (the more auspicious), where 'namah shivaya' occurs. Paraphrased. Confirm, and confirm Taittiriya Samhita 4.5 as the reference.
'These names are older than any sahasranama' rests on the Rudram being Vedic. A Keeper may prefer softer phrasing.
'Many people know this from their own lives' is about the listener's experience, not a claim about a tradition's members; check tone.
